cards.title: Light Changes Feel Faster Than Bodies Respond
cards.body: When lighting shifts suddenly, people notice at once. In this experiment, transitions between warm dim light and cool bright light quickly changed perceived brightness, color, comfort, alertness, and mood. But physiological measures such as heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance, and skin temperature showed little immediate response. The experience of light moved faster than many body signals.
cards.expanded_summary: Thirty-eight healthy adults completed four controlled sessions with different lighting trajectories: warm dim to cool bright, cool bright to warm dim, constant warm dim, and constant cool bright. Subjective appraisals changed quickly and often persisted, while comfort and acceptance showed adaptation over roughly 15 to 30 minutes. Performance and physiological arousal were less responsive than subjective experience. The finding matters for dynamic lighting: abrupt changes may make people feel more alert, yet they can also produce a temporary comfort cost.
cards.measurables: Measured or inferred through HRV, Heart rate, skin conductance.
cards.short_science_summary:
This card is about a controlled within-subjects experiment on abrupt lighting transitions and measures of alertness, arousal, comfort, and thermoregulation. Thirty-eight healthy participants completed four separate 90-minute sessions. The lighting conditions contrasted warm dim lighting with cool bright lighting. Some sessions included transitions from one condition to the other, while others held lighting constant.

The study measured several kinds of response. Subjective measures included perceived light intensity, perceived color temperature, visual comfort, visual acceptance, alertness, and mood dimensions such as calmness, happiness, and vitality. Objective or physiological measures included psychomotor vigilance performance, heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance level, skin temperature, and distal-to-proximate skin temperature gradient. The source claim specifically states that mean skin temperature and DPG were not significantly affected by the lighting transitions.

The main pattern is that subjective experience responded more clearly than many physiological indicators. People perceived the change in brightness and color temperature immediately. Alertness and vitality also showed immediate and persistent response. Visual comfort and acceptance were more complicated: transitions, especially toward cool bright light, could produce a temporary dip that recovered within about 15 to 30 minutes. In contrast, physiological measures such as heart rate, HRV, skin conductance, and skin temperature showed little rapid transition effect, apart from a gradual skin conductance increase in constant cool bright lighting described in the input as a possible slow activating effect.

This evidence is useful because it separates different meanings of response. A lighting change can feel powerful without producing a matching rapid physiological shift in every measured system. That matters for design claims. Dynamic lighting may help occupants feel more alert, but designers should not assume that abrupt lighting changes automatically create broad physiological activation during daytime exposure.

The limitations are important. The experiment took place in controlled daytime sessions, and the input notes that the findings may not generalize to evening or nighttime, when light can affect physiology differently. The lighting contrast was strong, so smaller everyday adjustments might produce weaker effects. The sample was modest, and the 90-minute session may miss longer adaptation. For practice, the prudent lesson is to use dynamic lighting carefully: transitions can be effective perceptually, but ramp speed, direction, comfort, and timing all matter.
cards.apa_citation: M.E. Kompier, K.C.H.J. Smolders, W.D. van Marken Lichtenbelt, Y.A.W. de Kort (2020). Effects of light transitions on measures of alertness, arousal and comfort. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2020.112999

cards.title: Bright Cool Light Wakes People Before It Comforts Them
cards.body: Abrupt light changes affect people quickly, but not all responses move together. In this controlled experiment, transitions between warm dim and cool bright lighting shifted perceived brightness, color temperature, alertness, vitality, and comfort. Alertness rose rapidly and persisted, while visual comfort and acceptance could dip temporarily, especially when moving toward brighter, cooler light.
cards.expanded_summary: Thirty-eight healthy adults participated in four 90-minute sessions with different lighting trajectories: warm dim to cool bright, cool bright to warm dim, constant warm dim, and constant cool bright. Subjective visual experience changed clearly. Objective physiological measures such as heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance, skin temperature, and distal-to-proximate gradient changed little, except for a gradual skin conductance increase in constant cool bright light. The asymmetry matters: turning light up is not simply the reverse of turning it down.
cards.measurables: Measured or inferred through HRV, Heart rate, skin conductance.
cards.short_science_summary:
This 2020 within-subjects laboratory experiment studied how abrupt lighting transitions affect alertness, arousal, and comfort. Thirty-eight healthy subjects took part in four separate 90-minute sessions at Eindhoven University of Technology. The lighting conditions contrasted warm dim lighting with cool bright lighting. The four trajectories were warm dim to cool bright, cool bright to warm dim, constant warm dim, and constant cool bright.

The study measured several kinds of response. Subjective measures included sensation of light intensity, sensation of color temperature, visual comfort, visual acceptance, alertness, and mood dimensions such as calmness, happiness, and vitality. Objective measures included psychomotor vigilance task performance, heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance level, skin temperature, and distal-to-proximate skin temperature gradient. Mixed models were used, with participant and session as random intercepts, and analyses compared transition and constant conditions across measurement blocks.

The main finding is that subjective visual and alertness responses were clearer than physiological arousal responses. Visual appraisals such as perceived brightness, perceived color temperature, comfort, and acceptance responded quickly to lighting changes. Alertness and vitality also responded immediately and persisted. However, comfort and visual acceptance could show a temporary dip that recovered within roughly 15 to 30 minutes. The input notes that fewer participants accepted constant cool bright light compared with constant warm dim light across blocks, which fits the broader pattern that brighter, cooler lighting can be activating but not always more comfortable.

Physiological measures did not strongly track abrupt transitions. Heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance, and skin temperature showed little response to the transition, with the notable exception of a gradual skin conductance increase in constant cool bright lighting that may indicate a slower activating pathway. This matters because designers should not assume that every perceived alertness shift reflects immediate broad physiological arousal.

For lighting design, the result supports dynamic lighting but argues for care in transition speed and direction. Cool bright light may rapidly support alertness, yet abrupt upward shifts can temporarily reduce comfort. Gradual ramping may preserve benefits while reducing disruption. The evidence is moderate: the design is controlled and within-subjects, but the sample is modest, daytime exposure may not generalize to evening, and the lighting contrasts were strong. The safest conclusion is that light transitions change experience quickly, while bodily arousal changes are weaker and more complex.
cards.apa_citation: M.E. Kompier, K.C.H.J. Smolders, W.D. van Marken Lichtenbelt, Y.A.W. de Kort (2020). Effects of light transitions on measures of alertness, arousal and comfort. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2020.112999

cards.title: Your Brain Perceives a Unique 'Hominess' in Architecture
cards.body: When we evaluate architectural interiors, our brains use three key dimensions. Alongside 'coherence' (how organized a space is) and 'fascination' (its richness and interest), researchers identified a novel dimension: 'hominess.' Unique to architecture, 'hominess' reflects a space's capacity to feel personal and comfortable. An fMRI study found that each dimension activates a distinct brain region, confirming they are separate psychological constructs. This provides a neurologically-grounded vocabulary for designers, showing that a sense of home is a fundamental, measurable component of our experience of interior space.
cards.expanded_summary: The discovery of 'hominess' is the study's most distinctive contribution. While coherence and fascination apply to our aesthetic judgments of natural scenes and artworks, 'hominess' appears to be a dimension tuned specifically for the built environment. It loaded highest on ratings of coziness, warmth, and personal space. The neuroimaging data, though based on a small sample (n=18), supports this distinction. 'Hominess' scores covaried with activity in the left cuneus, but only when participants made approach-avoidance decisions—a task related to judging a space for habitation. This suggests our brains possess a specialized mechanism for evaluating whether an interior affords dwelling and personal comfort.
cards.measurables: Over 1,400 participants rated 200 photographs of interiors on 16 aesthetic scales (e.g., beauty, comfort, interest). Principal Components Analysis (PCA) was used to extract the three dimensions. In a separate experiment, 18 participants viewed the same images while in an fMRI scanner, allowing researchers to correlate the dimension scores of each image with BOLD activation in specific brain regions.
cards.short_science_summary: Coburn et al. (2020) investigated the psychological and neural basis of aesthetic responses to architectural interiors. Across three experiments, they identified three fundamental dimensions that explain approximately 90% of the variance in people's judgments: coherence (the ease of comprehending a scene), fascination (a scene's informational richness and interest), and hominess (the degree to which a scene feels like a personal, comfortable space). The first two experiments (total N = 1,412) established this three-factor structure using Principal Components Analysis (PCA) on ratings of 200 interior images; the structure was robustly replicated in an independent sample. The study's most significant contribution is the identification of 'hominess' as a novel dimension specific to the built environment, as it does not typically emerge in studies of natural landscapes or artworks. In a third experiment, the researchers reanalyzed fMRI data from 18 participants who viewed the same images. They found that each psychological dimension covaried with activity in distinct brain regions. Fascination correlated with activity in the right lingual gyrus. Coherence correlated with the left inferior occipital gyrus, but only during beauty judgments. Critically, hominess correlated with the left cuneus, but only during approach-avoidance decisions, a task relevant to evaluating a space for habitation. These neural dissociations, which held after controlling for low-level image properties, provide strong evidence that these are genuinely separate psychological constructs. While the fMRI sample was small, the findings provide a neurologically-grounded framework for design, suggesting that architects must independently consider a space's legibility, interest, and its capacity to evoke a sense of dwelling.
cards.apa_citation: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors.

cards.title: Daylight may boost performance through visibility, mood, and health pathways.
cards.body: While studies show a strong link between daylight in buildings and better human performance, the exact reasons why are still being explored. Researchers suggest three potential mechanisms. Daylight can improve performance by enhancing visibility for tasks, improving people's mood, and supporting better overall health through pathways like circadian rhythm regulation. Understanding these pathways is critical for designing schools and offices that don't just save energy, but actively support the wellbeing and productivity of occupants.
cards.expanded_summary: A landmark study by Heschong et al. (2002) found students in classrooms with the most daylight progressed 20% faster in math and 26% faster in reading over one year. While the study established this powerful link, it could not isolate the specific mechanism. The statistical analysis controlled for over 20 variables like teacher quality and student demographics, but the reason for the effect remained unspecified. Subsequent analysis suggests several plausible pathways. These include direct visual benefits like reduced eye strain (visibility), psychological effects from a more pleasant environment (enhanced mood), and physiological impacts such as the regulation of sleep-wake cycles via circadian entrainment (improved health). This highlights that the benefits of daylight likely extend beyond simple illumination.
cards.measurables: This mechanism was not directly measured in the foundational study. Researchers instead correlated daylighting conditions with academic outcomes. Daylighting was rated by observers on a multi-point scale based on window area, orientation, and skylights. Student performance was measured by standardized test score improvements in math and reading over one academic year, controlling for confounding variables.
cards.short_science_summary: A landmark study by Heschong, Wright, and Okura (2002) provided strong quantitative evidence linking daylight in schools to academic performance. Analyzing data from approximately 21,000 students in over 2,000 classrooms, they found that students in classrooms with the most daylight progressed 20% faster on math tests and 26% faster on reading tests over one year compared to those with the least daylight. This large effect size persisted even after statistical models controlled for over 20 confounding variables, including teacher quality, class size, and student demographics. The study used a quasi-experimental design where trained observers rated each classroom's daylighting based on window area, orientation, glazing, and the presence of skylights. Student performance was measured by improvement in standardized test scores. The findings had significant implications, suggesting that architectural design is a powerful and cost-effective lever for improving educational outcomes, and influencing design standards like LEED. However, the study has known limitations. A key critique is that the mechanism for the effect is unspecified. The research established a strong correlation but could not determine *why* daylight improved performance. Researchers have since proposed several potential pathways to explain the finding. These include: (1) increased visibility, where better quality light reduces eye strain and improves visual comfort for learning tasks; (2) enhanced mood, where a daylit environment has a positive psychological impact on students and teachers; and (3) improved health, through physiological processes like the regulation of circadian rhythms which affect alertness and sleep. Disentangling these potential mechanisms remains an important area for future research.
cards.apa_citation: Daylighting Impacts on Human Performance in School.

cards.title: Indoor Nature Can Speed Recovery After Stress
cards.body: A plant-filled or nature-facing office may do more than look pleasant after a hard moment. In this virtual reality experiment, people recovered from stress more favorably in biophilic office environments than in a non-biophilic office. The strongest effects appeared early in the six-minute recovery period. The study makes nature indoors a testable recovery condition, not mere decoration.
cards.expanded_summary: Participants were stressed first, then assigned to recover in one of four virtual offices: a baseline office, an office with indoor greenery, an office with an outdoor view, or a combined biophilic condition. The researchers measured anxiety along with heart rate variability, heart rate, skin conductance, and blood pressure. Results consistently favored biophilic environments for stress and anxiety recovery, though the pattern differed by feature and outcome. The evidence is strongest for short-term recovery in a controlled simulated office, not for every real workplace or hospital room.
cards.measurables: Measured or inferred through heart rate, skin conductance.
cards.short_science_summary:
This card is based on a between-subjects virtual reality experiment testing whether indoor biophilic environments help people recover from stress and anxiety. The study used 100 participants and four virtual office conditions: a non-biophilic baseline office, an office with indoor green elements, an office with an outdoor view, and a combined biophilic condition. Participants completed stressor tasks and then spent a six-minute recovery period in one of the virtual offices.

The study measured both physiological and psychological responses. Physiological indicators included heart rate variability, heart rate, skin conductance level, and blood pressure. Anxiety was measured with a short version of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. This is important because the finding is not only about preference or visual appeal. The experiment asked whether the body and self-reported anxiety recover differently when the surrounding office contains nature-related features.

The input reports that participants in biophilic indoor environments had consistently better recovery responses than those in the non-biophilic environment. The effects on physiological responses were immediate, with larger impacts during the first four minutes of the six-minute recovery process. The three biophilic conditions did not all have identical effects, which matters for practice. A view, indoor greenery, and a combined condition should not be assumed to work in the same way or with the same strength.

The evidence is moderate and useful. Random assignment and a controlled VR setup make the comparison cleaner than many real-world studies, because the researchers can hold much of the environment constant while changing nature-related features. At the same time, VR is not the same as a real office, clinic, or home. The recovery window was short, the sample was specific, and the stressor was experimental. The result should therefore support design direction rather than a universal claim.

For design, the main implication is that biophilic elements can be treated as recovery-supportive environmental inputs. They may matter especially after stress has already occurred. This is stronger than saying people like plants. The study suggests that greenery and views can influence measurable recovery processes. Designers of offices, healthcare spaces, waiting areas, and other high-stress interiors should consider testing biophilic features against stress and anxiety outcomes, while keeping claims tied to context, exposure time, and the exact features used.
cards.apa_citation: Jie Yin et al. (). Environment International Effects of biophilic indoor environment on stress and anxiety recovery: A between-subjects experiment in virtual reality. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2019.105427

cards.title: The emotional character of a multi-colored image can be computationally modeled.
cards.body: Human emotional responses to the colors in complex images are surprisingly consistent. Research shows these responses can be modeled along three emotional axes: activity (e.g., dynamic vs. static), weight (e.g., heavy vs. light), and heat (e.g., warm vs. cool). This work extends a color-emotion metric from single colors to multi-colored images, turning a vague impression into a measurable perceptual field. This matters because it allows image databases and design tools to organize, search, and tune content based on predictable emotional impact, rather than just by object content.
cards.expanded_summary: The study validates a computational model for color emotion by showing that its predictions strongly correlate with human judgments. This suggests that the color composition of an image can be treated as an information-bearing variable for design, shaping perceived mood and similarity. The research was conducted in two stages: a pilot study with 52 observers, and a main study with a smaller group of 33. To prevent the smaller sample from being skewed by any single individual's judgments, participants in the main study were asked to judge each image sample only once. This careful methodology strengthens the finding that a shared, measurable color-emotion structure exists for complex images.
cards.measurables: The study used psychophysical experiments where observers rated 567 multi-colored images using category and interval scaling. Judgments were made along three emotion factors: activity, weight, and heat. The model's validity was tested by calculating the Pearson correlation between observers' average ratings and the predicted emotion values derived from the image's color structure.
cards.short_science_summary: This research investigates whether the emotional response to single colors can be extended to model responses to ordinary, multi-colored images. The study's core finding is that the color structure of such images can be effectively modeled using three emotion factors: activity, weight, and heat. Crucially, human judgments show a strong correlation with these modeled values, confirming that color emotion in complex scenes is a measurable perceptual field, not just a vague impression. This represents a significant step in developing computational tools based on emotional color response. The study employed a two-stage psychophysical design. A pilot study with 52 observers was followed by a main study with 33 valid observers. The methodology was adjusted for the smaller main group; to avoid any single observer influencing the data too heavily, participants judged each of the 567 image samples only once. Observers rated images using both category and interval scaling on the three emotion factors. The primary evidence is not based on p-values but on high Pearson correlation coefficients between the model's predictions and human judgments, particularly for the 'heat' and 'weight' dimensions. The paper demonstrates the model's utility for image retrieval and for organizing images in an 'emotion space'. The implications are significant for design practice and technology, suggesting that image databases and design tools can use color as an information-bearing variable to tune for specific affective outcomes. While the evidence is relational and not a single causal intervention, it strongly supports the model's validity within the context of this specific psychophysical study.
cards.apa_citation: Color Emotions for Multi-Colored Images.

cards.title: To make nightscapes feel safer, light the trees, not just the pavement.
cards.body: Outdoor lighting after dark does more than just make things brighter; it changes how a place feels. A Finnish thesis found that when light is focused on natural features like trees, people rate the scene as more restorative, safe, and pleasant. In contrast, when the same light is focused on urban features like parking lots or roads, ratings for restorativeness and safety drop. This suggests that the quality and focus of light—not just its brightness—can help make neighborhoods more supportive for mental recovery and recreation in the evening.
cards.expanded_summary: This research frames outdoor lighting as a tool for supporting mental recovery, drawing on Attention Restoration Theory. The theory posits that modern life fatigues our directed attention, and environments that support restoration can help us recover. The thesis used a series of studies with both simulated and real-world Finnish nightscapes to test this idea. By analyzing ratings of fear, preference, and restorativeness alongside qualitative comments, the author found a consistent pattern. Lighting that highlights pleasant, natural content supports the psychological conditions for restoration. This provides a new framework for lighting design that goes beyond simple visibility to consider the psychological impact of what the light reveals.
cards.measurables: The research was based on subjective assessments of both simulated and real-world outdoor environments after dark. Participants rated scenes on scales for perceived restorativeness, fear, preference, and pleasantness. In later studies, these quantitative ratings were supplemented with qualitative data from free-response comments. The Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS) was a key instrument, and its internal consistency was found to be high across all test images (Cronbach's α > 0.88), indicating its reliability for this research context.
cards.short_science_summary: Outdoor lighting changes how restorative, safe, and pleasant a place feels after dark. The thesis argues that people do not read light only as brightness. They read it as a scene cue that can support recovery, lower fear, and make a neighborhood feel usable. When light falls on natural or pleasant content, ratings of restorative potential rise. When light falls on urban or unpleasant content, the same people give lower restorative ratings and often more fear. The thesis combines a literature review with several empirical studies. It uses simulated scenes and field scenes, then asks people to rate restorativeness, fear, preference, pleasantness, and related lighting attributes. The design also includes free responses in later studies, so the author can compare numbers with open comments. The work uses ANOVA, linear regression, and appendix brightness checks, which makes it a multi-study thesis rather than a single lab test. That setup lets the author connect theory, scene content, and outdoor use after dark. The thesis organizes four studies on restoration, scene content, and focus of light. The abstract does not give one thesis-wide N, because the sample changes across chapters, but the thesis reports repeated significance checks at p < .05 and uses a mean age of 40 years in one field sample. The Roihuvuori and Herttoniemi studies compare outdoor night scenes, and the appendix brightness checks use 12 external raters with Friedman tests. Those details matter because they show both scale and caution, and they keep the chapter from sounding like a single anecdotal case. The main design move is to stop treating better lighting as just more light. The thesis argues for quality-based lighting that tracks scene content, user expectation, and neighborhood use. Natural and pleasant focal content seems to support restorativeness and safety, while urban or harsh content pulls the other way. That means designers should think about where the light lands, what the light reveals, and how the scene reads after dark. It also means near-home lighting can support recreation and recovery, not only circulation. The work stays close to Finnish nightscapes and to ratings taken from people who can describe and compare scenes. It also faces the usual risk of self-report: people may tell a story about lighting that is cleaner than the one their behavior would show. The thesis itself notes cultural, climatic, and scale issues, and some brightness judgments may depend on how the task was set up. The local record should keep that uncertainty visible and should not turn the result into a universal rule for every street or every climate.
cards.apa_citation: Perceptions of lighting, perceived restorativeness, preference and fear in outdoor spaces.

cards.title: Subjective perception of light, not just its brightness, affects mood.
cards.body: How you feel about your office lighting matters more for your mood than its objective brightness. A large cross-cultural study of 988 workers found that mood was highest when lighting was experienced as 'just right'. Mood declined when lighting was perceived as either too dark or too bright, regardless of the measured illuminance. This suggests that designing for subjective comfort, not just technical specifications, is crucial for creating healthier work environments that support well-being. These real-world findings demonstrate stronger, more nuanced effects than those typically found in laboratory studies.
cards.expanded_summary: This large-scale field study tracked workers in four different countries, revealing that context is key. In countries at higher latitudes, psychological mood varied significantly with the seasons, an effect not seen closer to the equator. The study also found that mood was linked to the distance from a window and that good colour design could contribute to a more positive emotional state. By moving beyond controlled lab settings, the research demonstrates that light and colour are not isolated factors. Instead, they are part of a complex environmental system. The findings push designers to consider the entire built environment as a whole to support occupant well-being.
cards.measurables: Researchers analyzed emotional responses from 988 workers using self-report scales. They used a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) to test how these mood scores were affected by factors like gender, age, and country. The study compared these subjective mood reports against both the workers' personal experience of the lighting and objective physical measurements of illuminance, finding that the subjective assessment was the more powerful predictor of mood.
cards.short_science_summary: This research aimed to determine how indoor lighting and colour systematically impact the mood of people in real work environments, moving beyond prior laboratory studies that typically isolated single variables. A large cross-cultural field study was conducted with 988 participants across four countries at different latitudes, with data collected across various seasons. The study's central finding highlights a critical distinction between objective environmental metrics and subjective human experience. While objective illuminance (measured brightness) showed no significant impact on mood, workers' subjective assessment of the lighting had a strong, non-linear effect. Mood was reported at its lowest when lighting was experienced as 'much too dark,' improved to its highest level when perceived as 'just right,' and then declined again as it became 'too bright.' The study also uncovered contextual nuances. In countries situated far north of the equator, a significant seasonal variation in psychological mood was observed, a pattern that did not appear in countries closer to the equator. Furthermore, the distance to the nearest window showed a bimodal relationship with mood, and the use of good colour design was found to contribute to a more positive atmosphere. The results underscore that in real-world settings, environmental factors have stronger and more complex effects than in labs. For design, the practical implication is that achieving a subjective fit of light and colour is paramount for occupant well-being. These elements should be treated as an active part of a complex system that makes up a healthy building.
cards.apa_citation: The Impact of Light and Colour on Psychological Mood: A Cross-Cultural Study of Indoor Work Environments.

cards.title: Neuroarchitecture Treats Design as a Biological Context
cards.body: Neuroarchitecture begins with a plain idea: buildings are not neutral containers for the nervous system. Light, color, sound, plants, materials, scale, layout, and volume may shape attention, stress, emotion, comfort, and social behavior. This review gathers that broad claim, while its evidence remains mixed and more suggestive than decisive.
cards.expanded_summary: The paper combines recent neuroarchitecture research with historical examples of architecture used to influence human experience. Its claim covers many design variables, including quietness, noise, daylight, color, scent, vegetation, spatial volume, and materials. The source claim notes that slightly scented plants were preferred for comfort, while quiet spaces improved attention and noise caused stress. Because this is a narrative synthesis rather than one controlled experiment, the right reading is cautious: the design variables are plausible levers, not guaranteed prescriptions.
cards.measurables: Measured or inferred through Narrative Review.
cards.short_science_summary:
This narrative review discusses neuroarchitecture, the study of how architectural features may influence behavior, emotion, health, cognition, and well-being. It is broad in scope. The paper considers design elements such as light, color, acoustics, material, scale, layout, volume, vegetation, and sensory qualities. It also draws on historical examples of architecture used to influence emotion and experience.

The useful idea is that a building is not merely a visual object. It supplies sensory inputs that people continually process while moving, working, resting, or interacting. Light can influence visual comfort and circadian timing. Sound can support concentration or create stress. Color and material may affect mood or appraisal. Scale, layout, and volume can influence perceived safety, wayfinding, social behavior, and comfort. Plants and natural elements may contribute through visual, olfactory, and attentional pathways.

The evidence discussed in the paper spans several kinds of claim. It refers to spaces with slightly scented plants being preferred for comfort, fairly quiet spaces improving attention, quiet spaces improving perception, noise causing stress, and natural sounds producing beneficial responses. These are not all the same kind of evidence. Some are likely based on preference, some on performance or perception, and some on broader literature about stress and restoration. That mixture is both the strength and the weakness of the review.

The strength is integrative. It encourages designers to treat environmental variables as part of human functioning rather than decoration. The weakness is that the article does not present a new controlled experiment with a single sample, exposure, and outcome. It cannot determine exact doses, boundary conditions, or mechanisms for every feature it discusses. Individual differences, culture, task, age, sensory sensitivity, and context may all change the result. A claim about one sensory feature also may not transfer to another building type or use case.

A cautious conclusion is therefore appropriate. Neuroarchitecture offers a useful framework for asking better design questions: what sensory condition is being changed, who is exposed, for how long, and which behavioral or physiological outcome is measured? The paper supports the view that design can affect well-being, but the strongest future evidence will come from studies that test specific features under clear conditions with measurable outcomes.
cards.apa_citation: , T. G. Avinash, , K. A. Althaf, , R. Varma Yadu, , K. Nowshad Shabeeb, , G. R. Raghav (2024).

cards.title: Dread by design: places feel creepy when they suggest a threat you can't see
cards.body: Some places feel creepy because they create a sense of possible but unseen threat. This paper, a narrative review, argues that dread arises from a combination of environmental cues like poor visibility (low prospect), an abundance of hiding spots (high refuge), and general mystery. These features trigger an evolutionarily-tuned caution response, keeping our attention active and our bodies on alert. This matters because it shows that "creepiness" isn't just a mood; it’s a cognitive and physiological reaction to architectural signals of ambiguous danger, relevant for designers aiming to create spaces that feel safe and comfortable.
cards.expanded_summary: The review connects prospect-refuge theory, ideas about our hypersensitive tendency to detect agency, and social cognition to explain this feeling. It suggests that places with blind corners, hidden recesses, and poor legibility can trigger the same unease as a haunted house. The key insight is that our bodies respond to these environmental cues before our conscious mind fully processes the situation. For architects and designers, this means that emotional tone can be shaped by carefully managing sight lines, escape routes, and the balance between intriguing mystery and unsettling ambiguity. The goal is to design spaces that invite exploration without triggering a primal sense of dread.
cards.measurables: As a narrative synthesis, this paper did not collect new data. Instead, it built a conceptual map by analyzing prior findings from research on prospect-refuge theory, environmental preference, social cognition, and low-frequency sound. The key evidence consists of recurring patterns and logical connections drawn from previously published studies, rather than new quantitative measures or experimental results.
cards.short_science_summary: This review argues that creepy places work by making a threat feel possible without making it fully visible. It treats the feeling of dread not as a simple preference, but as a place-based signal that something in the environment deserves attention. The paper synthesizes prior research to build a conceptual map, proposing that creepiness arises from a mix of low prospect (poor visibility), high refuge (many hiding places), mystery, and ambiguous agency—the feeling that someone or something is present. The paper’s method is a narrative synthesis, connecting findings from prospect-refuge theory, environmental preference theory, social cognition, and research on low-frequency sound. It does not produce new experimental data but arranges prior findings to explain why certain settings are unsettling. The authors show how architectural features like blind corners, hidden recesses, and poor legibility can trigger a physical caution response rooted in our evolutionary history of predator avoidance. The environment offers cues, the mind reads them, and the body reacts before language catches up. The key design implication is that architects can shape a space's emotional tone by managing visibility, escape cues, and the balance between mystery and legibility. Comfort often lies in a balance between shelter and openness, while creepiness appears when the balance tips toward uncertain refuge or a blocked view. The main limitation is that the synthesis draws from studies with different methods, so its conclusions should not be taken as a universal law. The experience of a place as “creepy” may also vary across cultures and situations.

cards.title: It's not the crowd, it's the closeness: personal space violations drive the feeling of crowding.
cards.body: The feeling of being crowded is not just about the number of people in a room, but about having your personal space violated. A classic experiment found that people felt more crowded when sitting close together, even in a low-density room. Interestingly, adding pictures to the walls reduced the feeling of crowding, but only for those sitting close. This suggests crowding is a two-step process: arousal from the personal space violation, followed by blaming other people. The pictures provide a distraction, changing the attribution and easing the stress. This matters for designing shared spaces like offices and waiting rooms.
cards.expanded_summary: To test this "two-factor" theory, researchers varied room density and interaction distance independently. In some conditions, they placed pictures and wind chimes on the walls as "attribution inhibitors." The results supported the theory: interaction distance was a stronger predictor of crowding than density. Supporting this, participants reported being more attracted to fellow group members in low-density conditions and when sitting farther apart. The pictures only helped reduce crowding in the close-interaction conditions, where the social threat was highest and a distraction was most needed. This highlights a key lesson for designers: managing personal space is the first priority, and visual elements can only mitigate stress when social cues are already intense.
cards.measurables: Researchers measured the experience of crowding using questionnaires administered after participants worked on two tasks in groups. These self-report instruments gathered ratings of the room, feelings of being crowded, and attraction to other group members. The study also measured task performance, time estimates, and punitiveness to see how the experience of crowding affected behavior and cognition.
cards.short_science_summary: This 1976 paper proposes a two-factor theory for the experience of crowding, separating raw density from the social interpretation of space. The theory posits that crowding occurs in two steps: first, an individual feels aroused by a violation of their personal space, and second, they attribute this arousal to the other people present. This model predicts that interaction distance is more critical than simple density in producing the feeling of being crowded. To test this, Worchel and Teddlie ran an experiment with student groups, varying density (high vs. low), interaction distance (close vs. far), and the presence of "attribution inhibitors" (pictures and wind chimes vs. bare walls). The team measured outcomes using questionnaires on crowding, group attraction, and other factors. The results strongly supported the theory. Far interaction conditions showed a significant density effect on crowding (F(1,32)=99.00, p < .001), but this effect vanished in close conditions (F(1,32)=1.96, ns), indicating that personal space violation was the dominant factor. The presence of pictures significantly reduced crowding, but only in the close-interaction setting (F(1,32)=23.04, p < .001). This suggests the pictures offered an alternative attribution for arousal when it was most intense. Participants also reported more attraction to group members in low-density and far-interaction conditions. For designers, the study implies that protecting personal space is more effective than simply increasing room size. Distracting or interesting decor can soften the stress of close quarters, but it is not a universal solution. The study's limitations, including a student sample and a specific lab setting, mean the findings are context-dependent, but they offer a foundational insight into the psychology of shared spaces.

cards.title: A room’s design alters how crowded it feels, regardless of the number of people.
cards.body: The feeling of being crowded is a psychological experience influenced by architectural design, not just the number of people present. In a lab study, participants felt that dark green rooms became crowded with fewer figures than light green rooms, even though the spaces were identical in size. This effect was strongest in rooms with high visual complexity when participants imagined a nonsocial situation. This matters because it shows that design choices like color and visual load can increase a space's perceived capacity and comfort, shifting focus from pure density to perceived freedom.
cards.expanded_summary: The research highlights a specific interaction between a room’s color, its visual complexity, and the social context. While light-colored rooms generally felt more spacious, the effect of high visual complexity was more nuanced. It significantly reduced the perceived space in dark rooms, particularly when participants imagined themselves in a nonsocial setting. In this condition—dark, complex, and nonsocial—participants placed figures representing themselves much closer to the exits. This suggests that complex visual information in a dark space can feel oppressive or confining, reducing one's sense of freedom and control, even without social pressure from other people.
cards.measurables: Crowding perception was assessed in a laboratory experiment using model rooms. Eighty undergraduate participants placed miniature clothespin figures into the models until they felt the space was 'crowded.' The key measures were the total number of figures placed and where participants placed the figure representing themselves. Researchers systematically varied the model rooms' color (light vs. dark), visual complexity (high vs. low), and the imagined social orientation (social vs. nonsocial).
cards.short_science_summary: This study argues that crowding is a psychological experience mediated by the built environment, not simply a function of human density. The research demonstrates that architectural variables can significantly alter how much space people feel they have and when they begin to feel crowded. Using a 2×2×2 laboratory design with 80 undergraduates, the study varied model rooms by color (light vs. dark green), visual complexity (high vs. low), and imagined orientation (social vs. nonsocial). Participants placed miniature figures in the rooms to mark their crowding threshold. The results showed that design elements directly influenced perception. The strongest effect was room color, which accounted for significant variance in figure placement (F = 25.116, p < .011); participants consistently perceived dark rooms as smaller and placed fewer figures in them before they felt crowded. However, the variables also interacted. A three-way interaction between color, complexity, and orientation was observed (F = 2.72, p < .1), with a key contrast emerging: in the dark green, high-complexity room imagined under nonsocial conditions, self-placement was significantly lower (χ² = 6.084, p < .05). This suggests visual complexity becomes particularly impactful in dark spaces, reducing one's sense of freedom. The primary design implication is that perceived freedom can be as important as physical floor area. By using lighter colors and managing visual load, designers can reduce the feeling of crowding and enhance comfort, even at a constant occupancy. The study's main limitation is its laboratory setting, which cannot fully replicate the dynamics of real-world crowded spaces. The student sample also limits generalizability. Nonetheless, the paper provides strong evidence that crowding is a felt relationship between people and place.
cards.apa_citation: Spatial and Social Aspects of Crowding Perception.

cards.title: Dimmer Classrooms May Help Memory Work Harder
cards.body: Bright classrooms are often treated as automatically better for learning, but this study points in a more complicated direction. In virtual classroom settings, lower illuminance was linked with stronger memory performance and different physiological signals. The finding does not mean all classrooms should be dim. It does suggest that light level can become part of the learning system, not just a visibility setting.
cards.expanded_summary: The study exposed participants to immersive classroom environments with different illuminance levels, then measured memory task performance alongside neurophysiological responses. The notable result was that lower illuminance, especially around 100 lux in this setup, appeared more favorable for memory than brighter conditions. Because the experiment used virtual environments and a specific memory task, the result should be read as a controlled clue, not a universal lighting rule. It asks designers to test learning spaces against actual cognitive response, rather than assuming that more light always means better learning.
cards.measurables: Measured or inferred through EEG, HRV.
cards.short_science_summary:
This card is about a controlled neuroarchitecture study of classroom illuminance, memory, and physiological response. Participants were exposed to immersive virtual environments representing university classrooms with different light levels. The study then examined psychological measures, including presence and memory performance, along with neurophysiological measures such as EEG, HRV, and EDA. The central finding is that lower illuminance, especially a 100 lux condition, was associated with better memory performance and changes in sympathetic or neurophysiological activation in this experimental setting. The input also reports that higher illuminance was associated with lower EDA-phasic values.

The important scientific point is not simply that dim light is good and bright light is bad. That would be too strong. The study instead suggests that illuminance can alter the cognitive and physiological state in which a student performs a memory task. Memory is not only a property of the student's mind; it is measured while the student is inside a sensory environment. If the environment changes arousal, attention, comfort, or neural activation, memory performance may change as well.

The evidence is moderate because the design connects a specific environmental variable to measurable outcomes, but the result remains bounded. The input mentions 142 participants overall and 40 in the main memory-task phase, and the setting was a laboratory experiment using virtual classroom scenes. That makes the study useful for isolating lighting effects, but it also means the findings may not transfer directly to every real classroom, every age group, every subject, or every learning task. The exposure window, the task type, and the virtual scene all matter. A short memory task in an immersive simulation cannot settle how lighting should be set for a full school day, a design studio, or a lecture hall.

For design, the result argues against treating illuminance as a neutral background parameter. It should be considered a controllable design variable with possible effects on memory and physiological response. A cautious practical lesson is that learning spaces may benefit from lighting scenarios tested against the actual use of the room. A reading task, memory task, discussion, and examination may not all require the same luminous condition. The study supports further testing of adaptive classroom lighting, especially where learning performance and occupant physiology can be measured together.
cards.apa_citation: The effects of illuminance on students' memory. A neuroarchitecture study.

cards.title: A stable viewpoint helps you reconstruct your path from visual motion
cards.body: When moving through an environment, the visual world flows past you. This 'optic flow' provides enough information to reconstruct your path, but accuracy depends on your orientation. Perception is best when you look where you are going, with your orientation fixed relative to your trajectory. A single, stable landmark can also improve accuracy. This matters for designing virtual environments or navigation aids, where providing stable visual references can help users better interpret their own motion.
cards.expanded_summary: In a study using head-mounted displays, subjects viewed simulated travel over a ground plane and then reproduced the path with a model vehicle. Their ability to reconstruct the path was good when their simulated orientation was fixed relative to the trajectory. However, when the simulated head turn (yaw) did not match the path's curve, subjects misperceived the trajectory. They tended to assume their orientation was fixed to the path, wrongly attributing the independent head turn to a change in the path itself. This suggests our perceptual system has a strong default assumption that we look in the direction we are moving.
cards.measurables: Researchers showed 32 subjects simulated 2D trajectories in a head-mounted display, with and without a landmark. Afterwards, subjects used a model vehicle to reproduce the path they perceived. The study recorded and analyzed errors in the reproduced position, orientation, and path shape to quantify perceptual accuracy under different conditions of simulated motion.
cards.short_science_summary: It is well established that human observers can detect their heading from optic flow—the pattern of visual motion experienced during self-movement—over very short timescales. This study investigated whether people can also integrate this information over time to reconstruct a two-dimensional trajectory. Researchers explored this question by simulating passive travel for seated subjects wearing a head-mounted display. The stimuli depicted movement over a horizontal ground plane, with some trials including a single landmark. The simulated trajectories were either linear or curvilinear, and the observer's orientation (yaw) was varied: it was either fixed in space, fixed relative to the path, or changed independently. After viewing each simulated manoeuvre, 32 subjects reproduced the perceived path using a model vehicle, allowing researchers to analyze errors in perceived position and orientation. The results showed that while subjects perceived their orientation (yaw) correctly, their perception of the travelled path was less accurate. Path reconstruction was good, however, under conditions where the simulated orientation was fixed relative to the trajectory. A key finding emerged when the amount of yaw was not equal to the path's rotation: subjects tended to perceive their orientation as if it were fixed to the trajectory anyway. This caused significant misperception of the path, as the independent yaw was wrongly attributed to a rotation of the path itself. The presence of a single landmark was found to improve perception, but primarily when it provided a fixed, stable reference point. The study's findings are constrained by its laboratory setting and simulated motion, highlighting the need for replication in real-world contexts. These results contribute to navigation research and have implications for the design of virtual environments, suggesting that stable visual references are crucial for helping users correctly interpret complex motion cues.

cards.title: Cultural background shapes how comfortable and calm a public square feels
cards.body: The same public square can feel very different to people from different cultures, even in similar weather. A study comparing Swedish and Japanese participants found that the Swedish group felt significantly calmer and more thermally comfortable. This challenges the idea that a single thermal-comfort target will work for everyone. Urban designers must consider that place experience is an intersection of physical exposure and social interpretation, meaning cultural context is as important as climate for creating pleasant public spaces.
cards.expanded_summary: This research highlights that psychological and socio-cultural factors can override purely physical climate measures. The study was conducted in public squares under comfortable thermal conditions (18-23°C PET), yet the cultural differences in experience were clear. Beyond feeling calmer, Swedish participants also rated the square as more beautiful and pleasant than their Japanese counterparts. These results suggest that people evaluate their environment through a 'cultural lens.' For international design practice, this means that a successful plaza in one country might not evoke the same positive feelings in another without considering local cultural interpretations and expectations for public space.
cards.measurables: Researchers gathered on-site evaluations from 106 Swedish and Japanese adults in public squares. While objective meteorological data was collected to ensure comparable thermal conditions, participants' subjective experiences were captured using self-report rating scales. These scales assessed emotional states like calmness, as well as perceptions of thermal comfort and the aesthetic quality of the square.
cards.short_science_summary: This quasi-experimental study by Knez and Thorsson (2006) investigated how culture influences the experience of a public square. The research compared 106 Swedish and Japanese participants' evaluations of squares under objectively similar thermal conditions, defined by a comfortable Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) range of 18-23°C. The core finding is that the subjective experience of the same physical environment is not universal. Despite comparable PET conditions, Swedish participants reported feeling significantly calmer (F(1,104)=5.07, P<.05) and more thermally comfortable (F(1,105)=7.77, P<.01) than their Japanese counterparts. The influence of culture extended to other perceptions as well. The Swedish group also rated the square as more beautiful (F(1,105)=8.03) and pleasant (F(1,105)=9.73). These results challenge the reliance on purely physiological or meteorological models for predicting human comfort. They demonstrate that people interpret their surroundings through a socio-cultural lens, meaning place experience arises from an interaction between physical exposure and psychological schemas. For urban design and planning, this serves as a crucial warning: designing for a specific thermal target does not guarantee a uniform emotional or perceptual outcome across different populations. To create spaces that feel pleasant and calm, designers must consider cultural context, social cues, and local attitudes as integral components of the design process, not just meteorological data. While strong, the study is bounded by its comparison of two cultures and its cross-sectional approach, which does not capture changes over longer exposure.
cards.apa_citation: Igor Knez, Sofia Thorsson (2006).

cards.title: Women's negative moods may be more stable than men's in changing light
cards.body: Your gender might influence how your mood responds to changes in indoor lighting. In an experiment, researchers measured participants' moods before and after they spent time in a room with either cool or warm lighting. They found a main effect of gender, where women's self-reported negative moods changed less than men's did. This suggests that the emotional impact of a built environment is not uniform; demographic factors like gender can moderate how people feel in a space, a key consideration for architects and designers aiming to support wellbeing.
cards.expanded_summary: The experiment involved 80 younger (~23 years) and older (~65 years) participants who were placed in an office-like room. Researchers also found an interaction between lighting and age on negative mood. Younger adults' negative moods were lower in warm light, while older adults' negative moods were lower in cool light. These findings highlight that lighting isn't just a practical detail but an "affective source" that can convey emotional meaning differently across demographic groups. The result argues for testing design choices against human responses rather than assuming a one-size-fits-all approach to creating comfortable and productive indoor environments.
cards.measurables: Researchers measured mood using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS), a self-report questionnaire. Participants completed the PANAS before and after being exposed to one of two lighting conditions in a controlled, office-like room. The change in their mood scores (delta score) was then analyzed to determine the effects of lighting, gender, and age on their emotional state.
cards.short_science_summary: Researchers investigated the impact of indoor lighting, gender, and age on mood and cognitive performance in a between-subject experiment with 80 participants. The study hypothesized that lighting is an affective source that may be perceived differently across demographic groups. Participants, comprising younger adults (mean age ~23.6) and older adults (mean age ~65.3), were randomly assigned to one of two lighting conditions in a neutrally furnished, office-like room. Mood was assessed before and after the lighting exposure using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS). An analysis of variance (ANOVA) on the change in mood scores revealed several key effects. A main effect of gender showed that females' negative moods were more stable than males' (F(1,72) = 4.48, p < .05). Furthermore, a significant two-way interaction between lighting type and age emerged for negative mood (F(1,72) = 11.76, p < .001). Younger adults reported a better mood response (less negative affect) in warm light, whereas older adults responded more favorably to cool light. The strength of the paper's main effects is supported by F-values as high as F(1,72) = 52.08 for other results. The design implication is that lighting is not a neutral background detail but a controllable variable that can influence human experience. The results suggest that effective environmental design should consider how demographic factors moderate responses to physical settings. However, the study's scope is a key limitation. The findings are based on a sample of 80 participants and a specific set of stimuli and tasks. Therefore, the results support a local inference, and broader generalizations would require further replication.
cards.apa_citation: EFFECTS OF INDOOR LIGHTING, GENDER, AND AGE ON MOOD AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE.

cards.title: Biomimetic design can make virtual exhibition spaces more engaging
cards.body: Commercial exhibition spaces can feel more intuitive when their design is inspired by biological forms. A study explored this by creating virtual reality (VR) spaces based on cellular structures and other natural forms. This 'biomimetic' approach combines design principles from nature with VR technology to test how people respond. The results suggest this method can create more comfortable and engaging environments, giving designers a way to fine-tune a space's feel before committing to a costly physical build.
cards.expanded_summary: The design process in this study drew inspiration from two biological levels. The first was cellular, analyzing parallels between cell structures and the flow of an exhibition space. The second was emotional, borrowing forms from nature to evoke specific feelings and make the environment more intuitive. By building these designs in virtual reality, researchers could quickly test and gather user feedback on the concepts. This workflow treats the exhibition space as a tunable system, allowing designers to iterate on abstract qualities like 'comfort' or 'engagement' based on user ratings before any physical construction begins, potentially leading to more successful commercial displays.
cards.measurables: Researchers assessed the effectiveness of the virtual biomimetic spaces using user questionnaires. Participants rated the designs based on their perceived comfort, enjoyment, and ease of use. Key evaluation metrics included scores for environmental adaptability (average 1.63) and authenticity (average 0.75), along with an overall evaluation where 85.5% of responses were positive.
cards.short_science_summary: This study investigates how combining biomimetic design—design inspired by nature—with virtual reality (VR) can improve commercial exhibition spaces. The paper's central argument is that spaces can feel more intuitive and engaging when designers borrow structural and emotional cues from biological forms, such as cellular structures. More than just a conceptual note, the research presents a practical design workflow that connects a specific methodology to user-rated outcomes, treating the designed space as an environment that can be tuned for better human experience. The proposed workflow first explores a "cell-like" design method, analyzing parallels between the operational dynamics of cellular life and the flow of an exhibition. It then incorporates "emotional biomimicry," using imitation and forms from nature to craft spaces that are intuitive and evoke positive emotional responses. These principles were implemented in a laboratory studio setting using VR. The effectiveness of the resulting virtual spaces was then evaluated by a visitor population through questionnaires that targeted perceived comfort, enjoyment, and adaptability. The evaluation yielded measurable positive responses. The abstract reports an average score of 1.63 for environmental adaptability and 0.75 for environmental authenticity. Overall evaluations were 85.5 percent positive. While the paper does not provide an extensive results section, these key figures demonstrate that the proposed biomimetic VR workflow produces more than just attractive concepts; it yields a quantifiable, positive user response. The practical implication is that designers can use biomimetic forms to create commercial displays that are easier to navigate and more enjoyable. The study also highlights VR's value as a fast and cost-effective design probe, allowing for iteration and user testing before committing to a physical build. However, the study's evidence base is thin, as the source paper is very short. The findings support a modest design claim but do not provide enough data for a wide causal story about all exhibition settings. The research is significant for demonstrating a measurable response, but its conclusions should be viewed as preliminary.
cards.apa_citation: Integrating Biomimetic Design and Virtual Reality Technology in Commercial Exhibition Space Design: A Biotechnological Approach.

cards.title: In home decorating, green is strongly tied to specific emotional responses.
cards.body: Color choices for the home carry emotional weight, but some colors are more strongly linked to specific feelings than others. A case study of Turkish residents found a significant dependency between choosing the color green and particular emotional associations (P=0.043); other colors tested did not show this strong a link. The study also found that emotional responses change with a color's value and saturation. This matters because it provides a practical cue for designers: the same wall color can support different moods, and colors like green carry strong, predictable associations in a home setting where comfort and identity are paramount.
cards.expanded_summary: The findings come from a residence-oriented field study where fifty participants matched adjectives to colors from a popular Turkish paint catalog. This design connects abstract color psychology to the practical context of decorating a home. While green's emotional link was the most statistically robust, the paper also reports that the blue family carries strong associations. Furthermore, demographic factors shape color perception, with age and gender being significant predictors for the selection of achromatic black. The results build a case for seeing residential color choice not as a simple poll of favorites, but as a nuanced process where color communicates mood, identity, and comfort.
cards.measurables: Researchers presented fifty participants with color samples from a commercial paint catalog during a decorating session. Participants matched a list of emotional adjectives to the color samples. The dependency between color choice, emotional association, and demographic factors (age, gender, education) was then analyzed using chi-square (χ²) tests.
cards.short_science_summary: This case study explores the emotional meaning of color choices within residential settings, moving beyond simple aesthetic preference to examine how color communicates and fulfills human needs at home. The research demonstrates that for this sample, color selection is tied to specific emotional associations, with the color green showing a particularly strong, statistically significant link. The study involved fifty participants from various age groups in Turkey, who were engaged in a residence-oriented decorating session. They were asked to match a list of emotional adjectives to a set of color samples from a popular commercial paint catalog. Researchers then used chi-square (χ²) tests to analyze the dependency between color choices, emotional labels, and demographic variables like age, gender, and education. The paper’s key technical evidence is presented in a series of tables detailing the frequency of emotional responses per color, demographic dependencies, and preferences by room type. Results showed a strong dependency between the choice and use of green and its associated emotional meaning (P=0.043), a distinction not found for the other colors tested. The study also reports that emotional responses shift with changes in a color's value and saturation, indicating that subtle variations matter. Furthermore, demographic factors were found to shape certain choices; specifically, age and gender were determining factors in the selection of achromatic black. While not reaching the same level of statistical significance as green in the dependency test, the blue color family also carried strong associations. The paper’s authors suggest that these findings provide a practical cue for designers and residents, showing that color decisions should not stop at style. The sample is modest and context-bound to a single national setting and commercial catalog, so its findings should not be interpreted as universal laws of color psychology. However, by revealing a real pattern in a field setting, the study effectively argues that in the home, color is a tool for shaping mood, identity, and comfort.
cards.apa_citation: Color-Emotion Associations and Color Preferences: A Case Study for Residences.

cards.title: The visual system uses five cues to perceive heading amid moving objects
cards.body: When you walk through a scene with moving cars or people, your brain must distinguish their motion from the background to know where you're going. A mathematical model shows how this is possible using five specific cues from the pattern of visual motion, such as the expansion or acceleration of objects. By combining these cues, the visual system can cancel out the visual 'noise' from moving objects, reducing heading perception errors from a potential 6-8 degrees down to just 1-2 degrees. This explains our robust ability to navigate complex, dynamic environments.
cards.expanded_summary: The model identifies five key segmentation cues: accretion/deletion (how objects cover/uncover the background), expansion/contraction, acceleration/deceleration, spatial curvature, and temporal curvature. The paper derives these cues mathematically from the principles of optic flow. It does not present new experiments, but instead shows that a linear combination of these cues can successfully explain the results of three previous psychological studies on heading perception. For example, the model demonstrates that acceleration/deceleration cues are highly effective, correctly distinguishing moving objects from static background features in 83-98% of simulated cases. This provides a concrete framework for understanding how multiple, redundant visual signals support robust navigation.
cards.measurables: This paper is analytical, deriving mathematical expressions for five visual cues from optic flow equations. The model's performance is not tested in new experiments but is evaluated by fitting its predictions to three published psychophysical datasets. The key measure from these datasets is heading bias—the error in degrees between a participant's perceived direction of travel and their actual direction—in the presence of independently moving objects. The model's success is gauged by its ability to reduce this bias.
cards.short_science_summary: Humans are remarkably adept at determining their direction of travel (heading) from the visual motion of the world, known as optic flow, even in complex scenes with independently moving objects (IMOs). This paper presents an analytical model to explain this robustness. It posits that the visual system does not need to fully segment a scene before calculating heading. Instead, it can use a set of five specific segmentation cues derivable from the optic flow field: accretion/deletion, expansion/contraction, acceleration/deceleration, spatial curvature, and temporal curvature. The authors provide closed-form expressions for each cue, showing how they can be linearly combined to cancel the heading bias introduced by IMOs. The model is not tested with new experiments but is validated against three published psychophysical datasets (Warren and Saunders, 1995; Royden and Hildreth, 1996; Fajen and Kim, 2002). The central result is that these cues are highly effective at distinguishing IMOs from the static background. For instance, acceleration/deceleration cues achieve 83-98% distinction rates. When the model incorporates these cues, it successfully reduces simulated heading bias from approximately 6-8 degrees down to 1-2 degrees, closely matching human performance in the original studies. The authors acknowledge limitations, such as using instantaneous flow fields rather than integrating over time, assuming simple IMO motion, and hand-fitting parameters to the data. The model also slightly overestimates heading bias by about 2 degrees in scenarios where the observer's and IMO's paths cross. Nevertheless, the work provides a powerful mathematical framework for understanding human navigation and offers concrete tools for improving computational vision systems in autonomous agents.
cards.apa_citation: Florian Raudies et al. (2013). Modeling heading and path perception from optic ﬂow in the case of independently moving objects. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnbeh.2013.00023

cards.title: Classroom Noise Research Often Misses the Student Body
cards.body: Classroom acoustics are often judged by decibels, but students do not experience sound as a meter reading. A scrape of a chair, a long echo, or hallway noise may affect attention, annoyance, and stress differently. This review argues that school sound research needs to connect the sound dose, the room, and the child's own physiological and psychological response.
cards.expanded_summary: The review found that many studies measure sound pressure level, reverberation, or speech clarity, while fewer also measure heart rate, EEG, pupil response, electrodermal activity, or student preference. That matters because the same measured level can feel different in different classrooms and to different students. A room's materials, geometry, ventilation noise, and social use shape what reaches the ear. The evidence is strongest as a map of missing links: it shows why acoustical comfort cannot be reduced to loudness alone.
cards.measurables: Measured through classroom acoustic conditions and outcomes such as performance, EEG, electrodermal activity, heart rate, and pupil response.
cards.short_science_summary:
This review examined how researchers assess students' acoustical preferences and needs in educational buildings. Its main point is simple: classroom sound is usually treated as a physical exposure, but students experience it as a combined physical, psychological, and bodily condition. The literature often measures sound pressure level, reverberation time, background noise, or speech transmission. These are useful, but they do not by themselves explain why a child may find one classroom tiring and another workable.

The authors organized the evidence into three broad groups. Dose-related indicators describe the sound itself, such as level, reverberation time, and background noise. Building-related indicators describe the setting that shapes the sound, such as room geometry, absorbing materials, layout, lighting, and ventilation. Occupant-related indicators describe the student, including perception, annoyance, preference, attention, heart rate, EEG, electrodermal activity, and other physiological or psychological measures.

The useful finding is not that one acoustic number predicts one student outcome. It is that the research field is fragmented. Some studies focus on noise dose, some on subjective annoyance, and some on physiological response, but relatively few bring these strands together in the same classrooms. That weakens the ability to explain real design problems. For example, two rooms with similar sound pressure levels may differ in reverberation, speech clarity, or background mechanical noise. Two students in the same room may also differ in sensitivity, age, attention demands, or stress state.

The source claim about two classrooms with different reverberation times and quiet versus noisy conditions fits this larger point. Performance effects in school settings are likely to depend on more than loudness. Reverberation, noise type, task difficulty, and the child's developmental stage all matter.

The uncertainty is important. The review does not present one pooled effect size or a definitive causal chain from classroom sound to physiology. It also notes that indoor soundscape research in schools remains relatively sparse. A careful conclusion is that acoustic design for education should use physical measurements, but should not stop there. Better evidence will come from studies that measure the room, the sound exposure, the student's reported experience, and bodily or performance outcomes together.
cards.apa_citation: Amneh Hamida ⇑ et al. (2022). Indicators and methods for assessing acoustical preferences and needs of students in educational buildings: A review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apacoust.2022.109187

cards.title: Time in nature provides stronger restorative benefits than other environments.
cards.body: Spending time in nature can restore your mental resources more effectively than other kinds of breaks. A pair of studies compared people's experiences in nature—like a wilderness backpacking trip—with non-wilderness vacations, time in a city, or just staying home. Participants who spent time in nature showed stronger recovery in both their mood and their cognitive performance. This suggests that designers can actively use natural settings to create environments that improve how people feel and think, rather than treating the environment as a mere backdrop.
cards.expanded_summary: The research used a two-study approach to test theories of restorative experience. A quasi-experimental field study compared experienced backpackers on a 4- to 7-day wilderness trip against those on non-wilderness vacations or staying home. A second, true experiment compared exposure to natural versus urban environments. The studies used a combination of self-reported mood, cognitive performance tests, and physiological measures to assess restoration. While results for overall happiness were consistent with some prior research, findings from a specific emotional-state measure (ZIPERS) did not replicate earlier studies, questioning their reliability. The convergent evidence from both self-reports and performance tests offers robust support for the restorative power of nature.
cards.measurables: Restoration was assessed using a multi-method approach. Researchers collected self-reports on participants' emotional states before, immediately after, and 21 days after their experience. Cognitive performance was also measured at pre- and posttest intervals. The second study added physiological measures to provide a more comprehensive picture of the restorative effects.
cards.short_science_summary: This paper explored different theoretical models of restorative experience through two studies that tied nature exposure to measurable outcomes. The research aimed to determine if experiences in nature produce greater restorative effects than other settings.
